sentences.text: Stokesosaurus were small, bipedal predators measuring approximately 3 to 4 meters in length.
A ridge on the ilium once thought unique to Stokesosaurus was also found on the holotype of Eotyrannus.
The type species Stokesosaurus clevelandi was named and described by James Henry Madsen in 1974.
The generic name Stokesosaurus honors the geologist William Lee Stokes.
The specific name clevelandi refers to the town of Cleveland, Utah.
The holotype, a left ilium from a juvenile individual, was discovered in the Brushy Basin Member of the Morrison Formation dating to the early Tithonian stage, approximately 150 million years ago.
The holotype consists of a left ilium belonging to a juvenile individual.
A right premaxilla was originally referred to Stokesosaurus but was reassigned to Tanycolagreus in 2005.
Later findings referred to Stokesosaurus included some ischia and tail vertebrae found in 1991 and a partial skull found in 1998.
A posterodorsally inclined crest on the lateral side of the ilium, a trait linking Stokesosaurus and Juratyrant, was also found in the undescribed left ilium of the Eotyrannus holotype.
A 2012 study classified Stokesosaurus as a basal member of the Tyrannosauroidea, closely related to Eotyrannus and Juratyrant.
A 2013 analysis placed Stokesosaurus and Juratyrant as derived members of Proceratosauridae based on a shared narrow preacetabular notch.
Stokesosaurus is classified within the superfamily Tyrannosauroidea.
Stokesosaurus is classified within the family Stokesosauridae.
In 1974, Madsen assigned Stokesosaurus to the family Tyrannosauridae.
Modern cladistic analyses indicate that Stokesosaurus holds a more basal position than originally thought.
Fragmentary remains possibly belonging to Stokesosaurus have been found in the Morrison Formation dating to about 152 million years ago.

The Morrison Formation, where Stokesosaurus fossils were found, spans from 156.3 to 146.8 million years ago, covering the late Oxfordian, Kimmeridgian, and early Tithonian stages of the Late Jurassic.
Stokesosaurus lived alongside gigantic sauropods including Camarasaurus, Barosaurus, Diplodocus, Apatosaurus, and Brachiosaurus.
Fragmentary remains possibly attributable to Stokesosaurus date to the late Kimmeridgian, approximately 152 million years ago.
Stokesosaurus lived during the Kimmeridgian to Tithonian stages, from 154.8 to 143.1 million years ago.
The Morrison Formation, where Stokesosaurus fossils were found, dates from the late Oxfordian to early Tithonian stages of the Late Jurassic, between 156.3 and 146.8 million years ago.
It is debated whether Stokesosaurus is a synonym of Iliosuchus, a hypothesis proposed by Galton in 1976 that he later withdrew in 1980 and which was not accepted by other researchers.
Benson and Brusatte debated that no bones other than the holotype ilium could be safely assigned to Stokesosaurus.
It is debated whether Stokesosaurus langhami is a valid species, as later studies suggest it should be placed in the new genus Juratyrant, leaving only the holotype ilium for Stokesosaurus.
In 2013, Loewen et al. proposed that Stokesosaurus and Juratyrant are derived members of Proceratosauridae based on a shared preacetabular notch with Sinotyrannus.
